title: Hop training vs. strengthening and stretching program: a randomized controlled trial on the effects on strength, function, and foot mobility in patients with plantar heel pain.
summary:
Plantar foot pain, commonly known as "plantar fasciitis," affects approximately one in ten adults. The discomfort is often most severe in the morning or after prolonged physical activity, significantly impacting quality of life. Common treatment strategies to date have included stretching and strengthening exercises for the foot and calf, orthotic insoles, and pain-relieving medications—typically with limited and short-term effectiveness.
However, recent scientific findings suggest that plantar fasciitis is less of an inflammatory condition, as long assumed, and more of a degenerative change of the tissue. This shift in understanding indicates that existing therapies should be reconsidered, with a focus on developing more functional approaches. Since the foot-calf complex plays a crucial role in stability and forward propulsion during walking, it seems reasonable to explore training methods that specifically enhance these dynamic functions. This study therefore investigates whether a simple hop-training-program, performed at home over six weeks, is more effective than a traditional strengthening and stretching routine.
The aim is to determine if the hop-training has a greater impact on mobility, muscular strength, and foot function in people with plantar heel pain, in comparison to a basic strengthening and stretching routine.

interventions.name:
Training Study (RCT):
Arm 1: Hop training (low-intensity jump training) as a home exercise program, performed on a daily basis for 6 weeks. The hop training has a progressive build-up and is based on the study by Ardakani et al. (2018).

Arm 2: (Control group) Strengthening and stretching program as a home exercise program, performed daily for 6 weeks. This involves a basic foot training program with strengthening and stretching exercises, based on a study by Thong-On et al. (2019).

criteria:
Inclusion criteria:
Plantar heel pain for more than three months prior to recruitment, pain on palpation of the medial tubercle of the calcaneus or the proximal plantar fascia and pain during the first steps in the morning or after prolonged inactivity.
Exclusion criteria:
Systemic pre-existing conditions, previous surgery of the heel or foot within the last 12 weeks, pregnancy, corticosteroid treatment in the plantar fascia within the previous 6 months, shockwave therapy within the last 8 weeks.
